HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Acute Cholec:
Overview — The Biliary Triad

Acute cholecystitis = inflammation of the gallbladder — the step beyond biliary colic where obstruction becomes sustained and infected.

RUQ painFever / ↑ WCCJaundice
Biliary colic✔✖✖
Acute cholecystitis✔✔✖
Ascending cholangitis✔✔✔
Pathophysiology — Calculous vs Acalculous
Unifying mechanism: Stasis → distension → infection — whether caused by a stone (calculous) or absent CCK stimulation (acalculous).
Calculous (90%)
  • Stone impacts in cystic duct / GB neck
  • → Bile stasis + GB distension
  • → Secondary infection by gut organisms
  • → Inflammation of GB wall
Acalculous (10%) — the "sick patient"
  • No stone — GB stasis + hypoperfusion + infection
  • TPN or prolonged fasting (ITU/critically ill): no food → no CCK → no GB contraction → stasis
  • Immunocompromised: secondary to CMV or cryptosporidium
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Constant RUQ pain — often begins as biliary colic then progresses; the constant nature is the key shift
  • Fever, systemic upset
  • Nausea, vomiting
Signs
  • Murphy's sign — inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation (GB descends onto examining hand)
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Murphy's sign — the examiner's fingers held at the right costal margin; on deep inspiration the descending inflamed gallbladder meets the hand, causing a sharp catch of breath (inspiratory arrest)
  • Guarding/tenderness (guarding → GB sepsis)
  • Tachycardia, tachypnoea — screen with qSOFA (RR ≥22, altered GCS, SBP ≤100)
Courvoisier's law: Palpable enlarged GB + painless jaundice = NOT gallstones — think pancreatic head / biliary cancer. Stones cause a fibrosed, non-distensible GB.
Investigations
Bloods
  • ↑ WCC, ↑ CRP (inflammation)
  • ↑ ALP (ductal involvement)
  • ALT + bilirubin should be normal — if raised, think Mirizzi's syndrome or CBD stone → MRCP
  • Amylase/lipase (exclude pancreatitis)
  • G&S if surgery likely
Imaging
  • USS — first-line: stones, distended GB + thickened wall, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Ultrasound of acute cholecystitis — a thick-walled gallbladder (>3 mm) with pericholecystic fluid and an impacted stone/acoustic shadowing, tender on probe pressure (sonographic Murphy sign)
  • HIDA scan — if diagnosis unclear; IV tracer → excreted in bile; cystic duct obstruction → GB not visualised
  • MRCP — if CBD stone suspected (↑ bilirubin or dilated duct)
Management
Initial conservative bundle
  • NBM, IV fluids
  • Analgesia + antiemetics
  • IV antibiotics — co-amoxiclav ± metronidazole
  • NG tube if vomiting
Definitive treatment
  • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — within 1 week (ideally <48 h of acute attack)
  • Always if complications develop
  • Not fit / not responding → percutaneous cholecystostomy (drain the infection)
  • Alternative: interval cholecystectomy at 6–8 weeks after inflammation settles
Complications
Within the gallbladder
  • GB empyema — pus; IV abx + cholecystostomy/cholecystectomy
  • Mucocele — mucus secretion from obstructed GB
  • Gangrenous GB
  • Perforation → peritonitis
  • GB carcinoma (chronic)
Ductal & beyond
  • Mirizzi's syndrome — cystic-duct stone compresses common hepatic duct → obstructive jaundice
  • Cholangitis — ascending infection
  • Pancreatitis — ampullary obstruction
  • Gallstone ileus — cholecystoduodenal fistula → stone in terminal ileum → SBO
⭐ Exam Pearls
Biliary triad
Colic = pain only. Cholecystitis = + fever. Cholangitis = + jaundice.
Constant vs colicky
Colic = intermittent, afebrile. Cholecystitis = constant RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's.
Murphy's sign
Inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation. Sonographic Murphy's on USS = focal tenderness over the visualised GB.
Acalculous = ITU/TPN
No food → no CCK → no GB contraction → stasis → cholecystitis. No stone.
Bilirubin rises → Mirizzi's
ALP up + bilirubin normal = expected. Bilirubin rises → CBD stone or Mirizzi's → MRCP
Courvoisier's law
Painless jaundice + palpable GB = cancer, not stones. Stones fibroses the GB wall.
HIDA scan
GB not visualised = cystic duct obstructed = cholecystitis confirmed
Management
NBM + IV fluids + co-amoxiclav ± metronidazole + early lap chole <1 week. Not fit → percutaneous cholecystostomy.
HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Acute Pancre:
Overview

Inflammation of the pancreas by enzyme-mediated autodigestion → necrosis. Commonest causes: gallstones + alcohol.

What this topic tests: Severity stratification (Glasgow score) — mild self-limiting vs severe necrotising are different diseases.
Aetiology — I GET SMASHED
LetterCause
IIdiopathic
GGallstones ⭐
EEthanol ⭐
TTrauma
SSteroids
MMumps (+ Coxsackie B)
AAutoimmune (SLE, Sjögren's, PAN), Ascaris
SScorpion venom, smoking
HHyper-Ca²⁺, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypothermia, hyperchylomicronaemia
EERCP
DDrugs (azathioprine, furosemide, valproate, mesalamine, bendroflumethiazide)
Pathophysiology
Final common pathway: ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → premature trypsinogen activation → trypsin → autodigestion → acinar cell necrosis → inflammatory cascade → (severe) multi-organ failure.
Alcohol mechanism
  • ↑ Zymogen secretion → thick juice → ductal plug → ↑ pressure
  • → Zymogen-lysosome fusion → trypsinogen → trypsin → autodigestion
Gallstone mechanism
  • Stone at sphincter of Oddi → obstruction → back-pressure
  • → Same trypsin activation cascade
Downstream consequences
  • ↑ Vascular permeability → third-spacing (3–6 L in severe disease) → drives aggressive resuscitation need
  • Circulating enzymes → fat necrosis → FFAs bind serum Ca²⁺ → hypocalcaemia (saponification)
  • Vessel autodigestion → retroperitoneal haemorrhage
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back — pancreas is retroperitoneal (the anatomical reason)
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Concurrent obstructive jaundice if gallstone aetiology
Examination signs
  • Epigastric tenderness, guarding/rigidity, low-grade fever
  • Haemodynamic instability (inflammatory response)
  • Cullen's sign — periumbilical bruising (retroperitoneal haemorrhage)
  • Grey-Turner's sign — flank bruising (retroperitoneal haemorrhage)
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey-Turner's sign (flank bruising) — cutaneous signs of retroperitoneal haemorrhage in severe necrotising pancreatitis
  • Tetany — from hypocalcaemia
Investigations
Bloods
  • Lipase — more sensitive/specific than amylase, longer half-life (better >24 h after onset)
  • Amylase — ~90% specific; does NOT correlate with severity
  • Both >3× ULN = diagnostic
  • ALT >150 → 95% PPV for gallstone aetiology
  • FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, glucose, lipids, Ca²⁺
Imaging
  • USS — early; assess for gallstone aetiology
  • Contrast-enhanced CT — oedema/necrosis; best at 6–10 days (too early misses necrosis); use in persistent inflammation or organ failure
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Contrast-enhanced CT of acute pancreatitis — a bulky oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding/fluid, and non-enhancing areas indicating necrosis in severe disease
  • CXR — pleural effusion, ARDS, exclude perforated ulcer
  • AXR (not routine): sentinel loop sign (dilated bowel loop adjacent to pancreas)
Severity Scoring — Glasgow (PANCREAS)
Assessed in first 48 hours. Score 0–1 = mild; 2 = moderate; ≥3 = severe. Also: CRP >150 at 48 h = severe disease.
LetterCriterion
PPaO₂ <8 kPa
AAge >55
NNeutrophils (WCC) >15 × 10⁹/L
CCalcium <2 mmol/L
RRenal: urea >16 mmol/L
EEnzymes: LDH >600 or AST >200 IU/L
AAlbumin <32 g/L
SSugar: glucose >10 mmol/L
Management
Medical (all cases)
  • A–E, assess fluid status + organ dysfunction
  • Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (balanced crystalloid; 3–6 L in severe disease)
  • Urine output target >0.5 mL/kg/h
  • Analgesia — IV opioids; avoid morphine (↑ sphincter of Oddi pressure)
  • DVT prophylaxis (LMWH)
  • Enteral nutrition within 72 h in moderate disease (gut barrier protection); do NOT make NBM unless vomiting
  • No prophylactic antibiotics (NICE) — broad-spectrum (imipenem) only for confirmed infected necrosis
Surgical / procedural
  • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — gallstone aetiology
  • Early ERCP + sphincterotomy (48–72 h) — biliary pancreatitis + cholangitis, CBD stone, or severe disease
  • Radiological drainage / necrosectomy — infected necrosis or walled-off necrosis with organ dysfunction; a step-up approach is used (percutaneous or endoscopic drainage first, escalating to minimally-invasive necrosectomy, before open surgery — PANTER trial)

ComplicationTiming / featureManagement
Peripancreatic fluid collectionEarly; no wall; mostly resolvesAvoid aspiration (precipitates infection)
Pseudocyst>4 weeks; fluid + enzymes in a fibrous wall, no epithelium (hence pseudo); retrogastricObserve ≤12 wks (50% resolve) → cystogastrostomy if persistent

Pancreatic abscessPus without necrosis; high fever + ↑ WCCDrainage

HyperglycaemiaIslet of Langerhans destructionInsulin infusion

HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Chronic Panc:
Overview
Chronic fibroinflammatory syndrome → progressive, irreversible destruction of pancreatic parenchyma. Unlike acute pancreatitis (which can fully resolve), chronic pancreatitis causes permanent structural and functional loss. The defining consequence: loss of both exocrine function (enzyme deficiency → malabsorption) and endocrine function (insulin deficiency → diabetes). 80% caused by chronic alcohol.
Aetiology
Most common
  • Chronic alcohol excess — 80%
  • Idiopathic — ~15%
Other causes
  • Metabolic: hyperlipidaemia, hypercalcaemia
  • Hereditary: cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutation), PRSS1 (hereditary pancreatitis)
  • Autoimmune: AIP (autoimmune pancreatitis), SLE
  • Congenital: pancreas divisum (ducts fail to fuse → impaired drainage), annular pancreas (head encircles D2)
  • Infection: HIV, mumps, rubella
  • Obstructive: pancreatic tumour, trauma, post-surgical
Pathophysiology — The Obstruction–Fibrosis Cycle
1
Inappropriate enzyme activation
Alcohol/other triggers → enzymes activated within acinar cells
→
2
Protein plugs in ducts
Protein-rich secretions precipitate → ductal plugs
→
3
Calcification
Plugs calcify → pancreatic stones (imaging hallmark)
→
4
Ductal hypertension
Stones obstruct duct → back-pressure → further acinar damage
→
5
Inflammation → fibrosis
Cytokine cascade → stellate cell activation → irreversible fibrosis → functional loss
Self-perpetuating cycle: each calcification worsens obstruction → more damage → more fibrosis. This is why it is irreversible even after the trigger (alcohol) is removed.
Clinical Features
Pain
  • Chronic epigastric pain radiating to back
  • Worse after meals (post-prandial pattern — secretin stimulates damaged gland)
  • Recurring acute-on-chronic flares
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Patient often leans forward to relieve pain
Functional loss — develops 5–25 years after pain
  • Exocrine insufficiency: weight loss, diarrhoea, steatorrhoea (pale, greasy, offensive, floating stools) — once >90% of acinar cells are destroyed
  • Endocrine insufficiency: pancreatogenic diabetes (type 3c) — brittle, hypoglycaemia-prone (no glucagon either)
Examination & complications
  • Soft abdomen ± epigastric tenderness; cachexia, severe weight loss
  • Pseudocyst → palpable epigastric mass → can cause biliary or gastric outlet obstruction, or become infected/rupture
  • Jaundice if common bile duct compressed by fibrosed head
  • Portal hypertension (splenic vein thrombosis)
Key differential — pancreatic carcinoma: new-onset pain, weight loss, or diabetes in a patient with known chronic pancreatitis must prompt re-imaging to exclude malignancy. Chronic pancreatitis itself ↑ risk of pancreatic cancer ×10.
Investigations
Bloods
  • FBC, CRP (inflammation)
  • Amylase/lipase — often normal or only mildly raised (burnt-out gland; unlike acute pancreatitis — key exam point)
  • Fasting glucose / HbA1c — endocrine insufficiency
  • LFTs — biliary obstruction from fibrosed head
  • U&Es, calcium (hypercalcaemia as cause)
  • IgG4 if autoimmune pancreatitis suspected (AIP — raised IgG4, responds to corticosteroids)
Functional tests
  • Faecal elastase — reduced (key exocrine insufficiency test; <200 μg/g of stool = insufficiency)
  • 72-hour faecal fat (gold standard but impractical)
  • Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E, K) — often depleted
Imaging
ModalityFindings / Role
CT abdomen (first-line imaging)Pancreatic calcification (pathognomonic hallmark), ductal dilation, irregular gland outline, pseudocysts, atrophy. Also excludes malignancy.
📷 Image placeholder — CT of chronic pancreatitis — coarse pancreatic parenchymal/ductal calcifications (the pathognomonic hallmark) with a dilated, irregular main pancreatic duct and gland atrophy
MRI / MRCPBetter ductal detail — "chain of lakes" appearance (alternating dilated and strictured duct). Preferred if no calcification on CT.
📷 Image placeholder — MRCP in chronic pancreatitis — a "chain of lakes" main pancreatic duct with alternating dilated segments and strictures
Abdominal USSFirst-line — may show calcification, duct dilation, pseudocysts; limited by bowel gas
ERCPDiagnostic (ductal anatomy) + therapeutic (stone removal, stenting, sphincterotomy)
EUSHighly sensitive for early changes; guides biopsy to exclude malignancy
Management
Stop alcohol — the single most important step. Slows progression even though damage is irreversible.
Exocrine replacement
  • Creon (pancreatic enzyme replacement) — taken with every meal and snack
  • Start 25,000–50,000 units lipase per meal; titrate to symptoms
  • Fat-soluble vitamins ADEK supplementation (malabsorbed)
  • Low-fat diet + small frequent meals
  • Dietitian referral
Endocrine management
  • Insulin for pancreatogenic diabetes (type 3c)
  • Brittle diabetes — high hypoglycaemia risk (glucagon cells also destroyed → no counter-regulation)
  • Annual HbA1c + ophthalmology, nephrology, podiatry screening
  • Metformin used with caution only
Pain management — the chronic pain trap
  • For acute flares: WHO pain ladder (paracetamol → NSAIDs → weak opioids)
  • Avoid long-term opioids → opioid dependence + hyperalgesia worsen the clinical picture
  • First-line for chronic pain: pregabalin (neuropathic agent) ± amitriptyline
  • Coeliac plexus block (EUS-guided) — for refractory pain
  • Optimise enzyme replacement (inadequate Creon → more post-prandial pain)
Endoscopic & Surgical Procedures
ProcedureIndicationWhat it does
ERCPDuctal stones, stricturesSphincterotomy, stone extraction, stent placement to decompress duct
Frey's procedureLarge ductal stones / dilated duct (>6 mm) with head diseaseLocal head coring + lateral pancreatojejunostomy — drains duct along its full length into a Roux-en-Y jejunal loop
Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy)Suspected pancreatic head malignancy, localised head diseaseRemoves pancreatic head, gastric antrum, D1+D2, CBD, gallbladder; reconstructs with pancreatico-, hepatico-, gastrojejunostomy
Total pancreatectomyDiffuse disease, refractory pain, hereditary pancreatitisComplete removal → brittle diabetes; sometimes with autologous islet cell transplant to limit endocrine loss
⭐ Exam Pearls
Irreversible fibrosis
Unlike acute pancreatitis (can fully resolve), chronic = permanent structural damage.
80% = chronic alcohol
Single most common cause. Other: CF, hypercalcaemia, hyperlipidaemia, AIP.
CT hallmark = calcification
Pancreatic calcification + ductal dilation + irregular gland = diagnostic.
Amylase/lipase often NORMAL
Burnt-out gland — unlike acute pancreatitis. Don't expect a 3× rise.
Two functional losses
Exocrine → steatorrhoea + weight loss (↓ faecal elastase). Endocrine → type 3c diabetes (insulin deficient).
Exocrine symptoms lag pain by 5–25 years
Pain comes first; steatorrhoea and diabetes appear only after >90% acinar destruction.
Faecal elastase = exocrine test
Reduced (<200 μg/g) confirms insufficiency. Key functional investigation.
Creon + ADEK + insulin
Core replacement therapy. Creon with every meal. ADEK vitamins supplemented.
Avoid long-term opioids — use pregabalin
Neuropathic agents for chronic pain. Opioids cause dependence + hyperalgesia.
Frey's vs Whipple's
Frey's = ductal stones (drainage). Whipple's = suspected malignancy (resection).
Type 3c diabetes = brittle
Glucagon cells also destroyed → no counter-regulation → high hypoglycaemia risk.
Always exclude carcinoma
Chronic pancreatitis ↑ pancreatic cancer risk ×10. New/changing symptoms → re-image.
HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Pancreatic C:
Overview — Exocrine vs Endocrine
Exocrine adenocarcinoma = 90% — the "pancreatic cancer" that is examined. Arises from ductal epithelium. 60–70% in the head (→ early obstructive jaundice), 20–25% in the tail (→ late presentation). 80% unresectable at diagnosis — vague symptoms mean late presentation is the rule. Endocrine (islet cell) tumours = 10% — rarer, hormone-driven syndromes (see below).
Risk Factors
Main risk factors
  • Increasing age (>60 peak incidence)
  • Smoking — the key modifiable risk factor (×2–3)
  • Chronic pancreatitis — ×10–20 risk
  • Family history / genetic syndromes (BRCA2, PALB2, Lynch syndrome)
  • New-onset diabetes (may be caused by the tumour)
  • Obesity, high red meat intake, low fruit/veg
NICE referral criteria
  • 2-week-wait: ≥40 with jaundice
  • Direct-access CT: ≥60 with weight loss + any one of: diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, new-onset diabetes
Clinical Features
Head tumours present early with obstructive jaundice. Tail tumours present late — painless, silent, and already advanced.
Symptoms
  • Painless obstructive jaundice — yellow skin/sclera, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus (CBD compression by head tumour)
  • Weight loss — cancer catabolism + exocrine dysfunction
  • Vague epigastric/back pain — coeliac plexus invasion or secondary pancreatitis
  • Acute pancreatitis as a first presentation (duct obstruction)
  • New-onset diabetes (red flag — tumour destroys islet cells)
  • Trousseau's sign of malignancy — recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis (paraneoplastic hypercoagulability)
Examination
  • Jaundice, cachexia, malnourishment
  • Epigastric mass (late)
  • Courvoisier's sign: painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = pancreatic/biliary malignancy — not gallstones (stones cause scarring/fibrosis, preventing GB distension)
  • Hepatomegaly (metastases), ascites
  • Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) if advanced
Key differential — cholangiocarcinoma: also causes painless obstructive jaundice. Distinguishing features: cholangiocarcinoma = biliary tree origin (hilar or extrahepatic); pancreatic cancer = pancreatic head origin. CT + MRCP + EUS differentiate.
Investigations
Bloods
  • FBC — anaemia, thrombocytopenia
  • LFTs — obstructive pattern: ↑↑ bilirubin, ↑ ALP, ↑ GGT; transaminases mildly raised
  • U&Es, clotting (biliary obstruction → ↓ vitamin K absorption → ↑ PT)
  • Fasting glucose / HbA1c
  • CA 19-9 — elevated in pancreatic cancer but also cholangiocarcinoma; used to monitor treatment response, NOT for diagnosis (poor specificity)
Imaging
  • Abdominal USS — first-line; shows pancreatic mass, dilated biliary tree, hepatic mets, ascites
  • CT abdomen + chest (gold standard) — triple-phase CT; defines tumour resectability (vascular invasion, lymphadenopathy, mets)
  • 📷 Image placeholder — CT of a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma — an ill-defined hypodense mass in the head with dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct (the "double-duct sign")
  • MRCP — biliary/pancreatic ductal anatomy; distinguishes from cholangiocarcinoma
  • EUS + biopsy — highest sensitivity for small tumours; allows tissue sampling for histological confirmation
  • PET-CT — staging, detect occult metastases
Management
Only curative option = radical surgical resection. Only ~20% of patients are resectable at diagnosis. Tumours classified as resectable / borderline resectable / locally advanced / metastatic.
Surgery by location
LocationOperationWhat is removed
Head (60–70%)Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy) + regional lymphadenectomyPancreatic head, gastric antrum, D1+D2, CBD, gallbladder → pancreatico-, hepatico-, gastrojejunostomy
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of the Whipple's procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) — resection of the pancreatic head, duodenum, distal stomach, gallbladder and CBD, with pancreatico-, hepatico- and gastrojejunostomy reconstruction
Body / tailDistal pancreatectomy ± splenectomy + regional lymphadenectomyPancreatic body and tail; spleen often taken (splenic vessels run with tail)
Chemotherapy
SettingRegimen
Neoadjuvant (borderline resectable)Gemcitabine or FOLFIRINOX → chemoradiation → re-assess resectability
Adjuvant (post-resection)mFOLFIRINOX preferred in fit patients (PRODIGE-24); gemcitabine + capecitabine (or gemcitabine alone) if not fit for FOLFIRINOX
Locally advanced (unresectable, no mets)Gemcitabine ± nab-paclitaxel
MetastaticPalliative FOLFIRINOX (if performance status adequate)
Palliative / supportive care
  • Biliary stent (ERCP) — relieves obstructive jaundice and pruritus (the symptom that most impairs QoL)
  • Creon (enzyme replacement) — exocrine insufficiency from duct obstruction / post-Whipple's
  • Insulin if pancreatogenic diabetes develops
  • Coeliac plexus block — for refractory pain
  • Nutritional support — dietitian, MUST screening
  • MDT: oncology, surgery, gastro, palliative care, hepatobiliary specialist nurses
Prognosis
  • Overall 5-year survival: ~5–10%
  • After curative Whipple's resection: ~20–25%
  • Median survival with metastatic disease: 6–12 months
  • Poor prognosis driven by: late diagnosis, early vascular invasion, lymph node spread
Endocrine (Islet Cell) Tumours
Functional tumours secrete active hormone → syndrome. Non-functional — no active hormone, present with mass effect or metastatic disease only. Often associated with MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1: parathyroid + pituitary + pancreatic tumours).

⭐ Exam Pearls
90% exocrine adenocarcinoma
60–70% in head → obstructive jaundice early. Tail tumours present late. 80% unresectable at diagnosis.
Courvoisier's law
Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = malignancy (pancreatic/biliary), NOT gallstones. Stones → fibrosis → GB can't distend.
Trousseau's sign
Recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis = paraneoplastic clue. Think malignancy (pancreatic, lung, other).
New-onset diabetes = red flag
Tumour destroys islet cells. NICE: ≥60 + weight loss + new diabetes → direct-access CT.
CA 19-9 monitors, doesn't diagnose
Also raised in cholangiocarcinoma. Use to track treatment response, not for primary diagnosis.
CT = gold standard; EUS + biopsy = tissue
Triple-phase CT defines resectability. EUS most sensitive for small tumours.
Head → Whipple's; Body/tail → distal pancreatectomy
Distal pancreatectomy often includes splenectomy (splenic vessels run with the tail).
Metastatic → palliative FOLFIRINOX
Biliary stent relieves jaundice. Creon for exocrine insufficiency. Coeliac block for pain.
Gastrinoma → Zollinger-Ellison
Severe refractory ulcers + diarrhoea. High-dose PPI. Associated with MEN1.
Insulinoma → Whipple's triad
Hypoglycaemia symptoms + BM <2.2 + relief with glucose. Most common islet cell tumour.
VIPoma → Verner-Morrison (WDHA)
Watery Diarrhoea + Hypokalaemia + Achlorhydria. Severe fluid loss.
Glucagonoma → necrolytic migratory erythema
NME = pathognomonic rash + hyperglycaemia + weight loss.
HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Cholangiocar:
Overview

Malignancy of the biliary tree — 95% adenocarcinomas. Generally silent until late; most are inoperable at diagnosis.

Anatomical classification (drives surgery)
  • Intrahepatic — within the liver parenchyma
  • Perihilar (Klatskin tumour) — at the bifurcation of left + right hepatic ducts; commonest site
  • Distal — distal common bile duct
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of cholangiocarcinoma sites along the biliary tree — intrahepatic (within the liver), perihilar/Klatskin (at the hepatic-duct bifurcation, commonest) and distal (lower common bile duct) — each dictating a different operation
Cross-references
  • PSC — main risk factor
  • UC — via PSC linkage
  • Obstructive jaundice + Courvoisier's law
  • Biliary colic differentials
Risk Factors
Unifying theme: Chronic biliary inflammation → malignant transformation. PSC, liver flukes, and congenital duct dilation all funnel through this mechanism.
Key risk factors
  • PSC (primary sclerosing cholangitis) — the main risk factor; chronic ductal scarring and inflammation
  • UC — PSC ↔ UC are strongly linked
  • Liver flukes (e.g. Clonorchis sinensis) — explains ↑ incidence in SE Asia
  • HIV, viral hepatitis (B/C)
Congenital & other
  • Caroli's disease — intrahepatic duct dilation
  • Choledochal cyst — bile duct dilation
  • Rubber/aircraft industry chemicals
  • Alcohol excess, diabetes
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Generally asymptomatic until late
  • Painless obstructive jaundice + pruritus + dark urine + pale stools + steatorrhoea
  • RUQ pain (persistent biliary-colic-type after fatty meals)
  • Advanced: weight loss, lethargy, anorexia
Examination — malignancy cluster
  • Jaundice + cachexia
  • Palpable GB + painless jaundice → Courvoisier's law (cancer, not stones)
  • Virchow's node — left supraclavicular (Troisier's sign, GI malignancy)
  • Sister Mary Joseph node — periumbilical (intra-abdominal spread)
Investigations
Diagnosis requires both imaging AND histology.
Bloods & markers
  • Obstructive LFTs: ↑ bilirubin, ↑ ALP, ↑ GGT
  • ↑ CA19-9 — the key biliary tumour marker
  • ↑ CEA
Imaging & tissue
  • CT TAP — staging modality of choice (metastases + resectability)
  • Angiography — pre-op vascular mapping (hepatic arteries, portal vein)
  • ERCP — tissue (brushings) + delineates exact location
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Cholangiogram/MRCP of a perihilar (Klatskin) cholangiocarcinoma — a stricture at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts with dilated intrahepatic ducts above it
  • USS — dilated biliary tree (initial)
Management
Only definitive cure = complete surgical resection. But most are inoperable at diagnosis, and ~50% recur by 5 years even after resection.
Tumour siteOperation
Intrahepatic / Klatskin (perihilar)Partial hepatectomy + biliary tree reconstruction
Distal common ductPancreaticoduodenectomy — Whipple's or PPPD (pylorus-preserving) ± adjuvant/neoadjuvant radiotherapy
Palliative (majority of patients)
  • ERCP stenting — commonest palliative act; relieves obstructive jaundice
  • Surgical bypass if stenting fails
  • Palliative chemotherapy — first-line gemcitabine + cisplatin, now with durvalumab (immunotherapy) added (TOPAZ-1); targeted therapy for intrahepatic tumours with FGFR2 fusions (pemigatinib) or IDH1 mutations (ivosidenib)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Klatskin tumour
Perihilar = hepatic duct bifurcation = commonest site
PSC = main RF
PSC ↔ UC strongly linked. Liver flukes explain SE Asian incidence.
Courvoisier's law
Painless jaundice + palpable GB = cancer, not stones
Spread signs
Virchow's (left supraclavicular) + Sister Mary Joseph (periumbilical) = malignant spread
CA19-9
Key biliary tumour marker. Obstructive LFTs: ↑ bili + ↑ ALP + ↑ GGT.
Diagnosis = imaging + histology
CT TAP for staging; ERCP for tissue (brushings)
Resection by site
Hilar → hepatectomy. Distal → Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy).
Most are inoperable
Palliate with ERCP stent to relieve jaundice — the commonest intervention
HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Biliary Coli:
Overview — The Obstruction/Inflammation Fork

Biliary colic = pain from the gallbladder contracting against a stone transiently obstructing the cystic duct — temporary obstruction, no inflammation.

📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of the biliary tree — cystic duct, common hepatic and common bile ducts, and the ampulla — showing where an impacted stone produces each syndrome (cystic duct → colic/cholecystitis; CBD → cholangitis; ampulla → gallstone pancreatitis)
ObstructionInflammation/infectionFever / ↑ WCC
Biliary colicTransientNoNo
Acute cholecystitisCystic duct (sustained)Yes (GB wall)Yes
Ascending cholangitisCBDYes (infected bile)Yes + jaundice
Pathology — Stone Types

Bile = cholesterol + phospholipids + bile pigments. Cholesterol is kept soluble by bile salts + phospholipids (micelles). Tip that balance → cholesterol precipitates → stones.

TypeCompositionDriven by
CholesterolPure cholesterolExcess cholesterol or bile-salt deficiency; GB stasis / ↓ motility
PigmentBilirubin polymers + calcium bilirubinateChronic haemolysis (sickle cell, spherocytosis); duct strictures
MixedBoth—
Risk Factors
The four F's
  • Fat
  • Female
  • Fertile
  • Forty
Other risk factors
  • Pregnancy / OCP — oestrogen ↑ biliary cholesterol secretion
  • Diabetes, rapid weight loss
  • Crohn's / ileal resection — bile salts not reabsorbed at terminal ileum → deficiency
  • Drugs: fibrates, OCP
Clinical Features — Biliary Colic
Symptoms
  • Colicky RUQ pain — severe, recurrent episodes
  • Precipitated by fatty food → CCK release → GB contraction against the stone
  • Radiates to right shoulder / subscapular (referred via phrenic/diaphragm)
  • Nausea and vomiting
Defining negatives (vs cholecystitis)
  • No fever
  • Normal inflammatory markers (CRP, WCC)
  • Normal LFTs between attacks
  • No peritonism / Murphy's sign
Investigations & Management
Investigations
  • Transabdominal USS — first-line: stones/sludge, GB wall thickness, bile duct dilation
  • 📷 Image placeholder — Gallbladder ultrasound — an echogenic gallstone with posterior acoustic shadowing within the gallbladder lumen
  • MRCP — if USS inconclusive, or to image the CBD (↑ LFTs / dilated duct)
  • Bloods: LFTs are typically normal in biliary colic (transient cystic-duct obstruction). Raised ALP + bilirubin (obstruction pattern) instead points to a CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) → image the duct with MRCP
Management
  • Analgesia: paracetamol ± NSAIDs ± opiates
  • Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy — definitive for symptomatic disease (asymptomatic gallstones in a normal gallbladder need no treatment — reassure; NICE CG188)
  • Abnormal LFTs or dilated CBD → pre-op MRCP
  • CBD stones → ERCP (before or during cholecystectomy)
The logic: ERCP for the duct, cholecystectomy for the gallbladder — addressed separately.

The three presentations
Colic = pain only (no fever, normal markers). Cholecystitis = + Murphy's + inflammation. Cholangitis = + Charcot's triad.
Fatty food → pain
Fatty acids → CCK → GB contraction against stone. The mechanism behind the classic history.
Four F's
Fat · Female · Fertile · Forty

HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__Ascending Ch:
Overview — The Biliary Triad Completed

Ascending cholangitis = bacterial infection of the biliary tree — the third and most dangerous step, requiring both obstruction and infection.

RUQ painFever / ↑ WCCJaundice
Biliary colic✔✖✖
Acute cholecystitis✔✔✖
Ascending cholangitis✔✔✔
Two-hit requirement: Obstruction + infection — neither alone causes cholangitis. Commonest organism: E. coli ("E.scending coli-angitis"), then Klebsiella, Enterococcus.
Causes & Pathophysiology
Causes of biliary obstruction
  • Gallstones (commonest)
  • ERCP / biliary instrumentation (iatrogenic)
  • Cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatitis
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
  • Parasitic infection
Pathophysiology
  • Biliary stasis + raised intraluminal pressure → bacterial colonisation becomes pathological
  • ↑ Pressure drives bacteria/toxins back into bloodstream → sepsis
  • Without obstruction, colonisation alone rarely causes cholangitis
Clinical Features — Triad to Pentad
Charcot's triad
  • RUQ pain
  • Fever
  • Jaundice
Reynolds pentad = septic shock
  • Charcot's triad +
  • Hypotension
  • Confusion
Obstructive jaundice picture: Pruritus, pale/clay-coloured stool, dark urine. History clues: gallstones, recent ERCP/biliary instrumentation, lipid-rich diet.
Investigations
Bloods
  • ↑ WCC (leucocytosis), ↑ CRP
  • Obstructive LFTs: ↑ ALP ± GGT, ↑ bilirubin
  • Blood cultures — before antibiotics
Imaging
  • USS — bile duct dilation + duct stones (first-line)
  • ERCP = gold standard — diagnostic and therapeutic (the defining feature)
  • 📷 Image placeholder — ERCP cholangiogram in ascending cholangitis — a dilated common bile duct with a filling defect (stone), treated at the same sitting by sphincterotomy, stone extraction and stent placement
  • MRCP — if ERCP not immediately available; images the biliary tree non-invasively
  • 📷 Image placeholder — MRCP of the biliary tree — non-invasive imaging showing a dilated common bile duct with an obstructing stone as a filling defect
Management
This is a septic emergency. Treat as sepsis first, then decompress the duct. Antibiotics alone don't cure it — the obstruction must be relieved.
1. Immediate — treat the sepsis
  • IV access, fluid resuscitation
  • Blood cultures, bloods
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics: co-amoxiclav + metronidazole
  • Apply Sepsis Six framework
2. Definitive — biliary decompression
  • ERCP ± sphincterotomy + stenting at 24–48 h — first-line after stabilisation (timing depends on severity — urgent/emergency decompression if septic shock / Reynolds pentad / failure to respond, per Tokyo Guidelines)
  • ERCP can: image the tree, remove stones, dilate strictures, place stents, take biopsies
  • PTC (percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography) — 2nd-line if ERCP fails/inaccessible; radiological drain through skin + liver
ERCP complications: Acute pancreatitis (commonest), bleeding, perforation, repeated cholangitis.

RUQ pain + fever + jaundice
Reynolds pentad
Charcot's + hypotension + confusion = septic shock — escalate immediately

Obstructive LFTs

ERCP = gold standard
Diagnostic AND therapeutic. USS + MRCP to image; ERCP to treat.
ERCP → pancreatitis

Management order
